name: MAX and Mojo (Modular)
license: Apache-2.0 with LLVM Exceptions (the LICENSE file states this; the GitHub API reports NOASSERTION)
production_evidence: NO INDEPENDENT PRODUCTION EVIDENCE FOUND. The vendor publishes a hosted inference product and an enterprise 'schedule a demo' path, which is commercial availability rather than third-party production use. This is a false, not an omission, because no third-party production deployment is documented in any source reachable here
strengths: One package across NVIDIA, AMD and Apple silicon with no CUDA-version matching and no hardware selection at install time - the vendor states 'no CUDA version to match, no hardware option to select'
Does not depend on PyTorch, CUDA or ROCm, so containers are smaller and cold starts faster, per the vendor

Mojo exposes MLIR directly: four built-ins (__mlir_type, __mlir_attr, __mlir_op, __mlir_region) let a kernel author emit an operation Mojo does not surface - the docs name NVVM barriers, AMD matrix multiplies and target-specific address spaces
All MAX Python API, model pipelines and GPU kernels for NVIDIA, AMD and Apple are open sourced
Explicit GPU compatibility check: DeviceContext() 'raises an error if no compatible GPU is available' rather than failing later
weaknesses: The portability claim is entirely vendor-published with no third-party cross-vendor benchmark behind it in any source found here
MLIR is exposed to users, which is a strength for reaching hardware and a liability for stability: Mojo's semantics change with the upstream MLIR it is built on
No autotuner documented - performance is whatever the compiler's own scheduling and the shipped kernel library achieve
Youngest toolchain here and the smallest deployment base: a 2023 repo with no published third-party production case study
Serving and modelling APIs are young, and the Python-like surface will not map a team existing PyTorch expertise one-for-one
notes: Recorded as a compiler, not an engine, on the strength of the two facts that make it one: MAX compiles model graphs down across three hardware families from one package, and Mojo is a frontend onto MLIR rather than a closed DSL. The inline-MLIR escape hatch is the part most likely to matter to a kernel author and the part easiest to miss - Mojo's documented answer to 'this operation is not exposed' is 'write the MLIR op yourself', which makes it a Python-shaped MLIR frontend rather than a language with its own dialect design. PRODUCTION_READY IS FALSE, DELIBERATELY, and this is the one production_ready value in this batch that is a negative claim rather than an omission. Modular sells hosted inference and demos to enterprises, and a less careful pass would have recorded 'yes' on the strength of that; but production_ready in this schema means used in production INFERENCE ENGINES, and no third-party engine deployment or independent measurement is documented in any source reachable here. A vendor product page is not production evidence, and recording it as such would be the exact vendor-claim-as-fact error AGENTS.md's contract exists to prevent. If a third-party production deployment appears, this flips to true with the source named. output_artifacts carries mlir-ir, which is NOT in this schema's documented enum (ptx, amdgcn, spirv, air, metal, c, llvm-ir, triton-ir, cubin, plan) - flagged here as enum debt rather than presented as a listed value, because Mojo genuinely does emit MLIR and the enum genuinely does not describe it. validate.py does not enforce item enums on arrays, which is why it passes; that is a validator gap, not a licence to invent. compile_time_seconds is null: no primary source publishes a per-kernel compile time. confidence is 0.8 for the mechanism and materially lower for the performance story, which rests entirely on vendor claims.
